## 1. The garden on raised ground  (`#the-garden-on-raised-ground`)

Cited ayat: 2:265-266

> **2:265** وَمَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ أَمْوَٰلَهُمُ ٱبْتِغَآءَ مَرْضَاتِ ٱللَّهِ وَتَثْبِيتًا مِّنْ أَنفُسِهِمْ كَمَثَلِ جَنَّةٍۭ بِرَبْوَةٍ أَصَابَهَا وَابِلٌ فَـَٔاتَتْ أُكُلَهَا ضِعْفَيْنِ فَإِن لَّمْ يُصِبْهَا وَابِلٌ فَطَلٌّ وَٱللَّهُ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ بَصِيرٌ
>
> **2:266** أَيَوَدُّ أَحَدُكُمْ أَن تَكُونَ لَهُۥ جَنَّةٌ مِّن نَّخِيلٍ وَأَعْنَابٍ تَجْرِى مِن تَحْتِهَا ٱلْأَنْهَٰرُ لَهُۥ فِيهَا مِن كُلِّ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ وَأَصَابَهُ ٱلْكِبَرُ وَلَهُۥ ذُرِّيَّةٌ ضُعَفَآءُ فَأَصَابَهَآ إِعْصَارٌ فِيهِ نَارٌ فَٱحْتَرَقَتْ كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمُ ٱلْـَٔايَٰتِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَفَكَّرُونَ

### Claims

**c1** (2:265): The ayah gives a similitude of those who spend their wealth seeking God's approval and out of firmness within themselves: it is like a garden on raised ground (rabwa) that a heavy rain strikes, so that it gave its produce doubled, and if no heavy rain strikes it, then a light dew.

**c2** (2:265): The ayah ends by saying that God sees what they do.

**c3** (2:266): The next ayah asks whether any of those addressed would like to have a garden of date palms and vines, with rivers flowing beneath it and every kind of fruit in it, and then old age strikes him while his offspring are weak, and a whirlwind with fire in it strikes the garden and it burns.

**c4** (2:266): The ayah ends by saying that thus God makes the signs clear to them, that they may reflect.

### One-minute summary

The ayah likens those who spend their wealth seeking God's approval to a garden on raised ground that gave its produce doubled after a heavy rain [c1]. The next ayah asks whether anyone would like a garden that a whirlwind with fire in it burns, when old age has struck him and his offspring are weak [c3].

### Complete story

The ayah gives a similitude of those who spend their wealth seeking God's approval and out of firmness within themselves [c1]. They are like a garden on raised ground that a heavy rain strikes, so that it gave its produce doubled [c1]. If no heavy rain strikes it, then a light dew falls [c1]. The ayah ends by saying that God sees what they do [c2].

The next ayah asks whether any of those addressed would like to have a garden of date palms and vines, with rivers flowing beneath it and every kind of fruit in it [c3]. It goes on that old age strikes him while his offspring are weak, and a whirlwind with fire in it strikes the garden and it burns [c3]. The ayah ends by saying that thus God makes the signs clear to them, that they may reflect [c4].

### Deep study

The first ayah names what is likened (spending seeking God's approval and out of firmness within themselves) and what it is likened to (a garden on raised ground) [c1]. The next ayah is put as a question and does not itself say what the garden and the whirlwind stand for [c3]. The ayat close by saying that God sees what they do and that He makes the signs clear [c2][c4].

### Kids mode

Those who spend to seek God's approval are likened to a garden on raised ground [c1]. A heavy rain makes it give doubled produce, and if no heavy rain strikes it, a light dew falls [c1]. God sees what people do [c2].

### Life lessons (educational interpretation)

Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture of the garden on raised ground shows a garden that gives something either way, whether a heavy rain or a light dew falls on it [c1]. Another reading is that the picture of the burned garden is a question the listener is asked to consider, and that the ayat end by saying God makes the signs clear so that they may reflect [c3][c4].

### What the sources do not establish

- Not established: who is meant by those who spend beyond the description in the ayah; no person is named.
- Not established: who the man with the burned garden is, or what the fire and the whirlwind stand for; the ayah poses a question and gives no key.
- The first ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal). The next ayah does not use it: that it is grouped with the first as a parable is the platform's classification, not the text's.
- The words rabwa (raised ground) and tathbit min anfusihim (firmness within themselves, or confirming their own souls) are read in more than one way; this draft keeps the wording general.
